Katalog Berita (Halaman 38/57)

#4000. "We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly": Epic get more specific about genAI use in Unreal Engine and Fortnite development

Epic Games are, dunno if you've heard, on a bit of a genAI kick at the moment. It's been tough to notice unless you listen very hard. Tim Sweeney's lips have been sealed and no reports have spewed forth.

Sark aside, to this point Epic have had far more provocative soundbites and weird marketing lingo to offer than specific detail about how they're using genAI in different parts of their business.

Responding to questioning from This Week in Videogames, Epic's executive vice president of development Marcus Wassmer's run through some of the exact tools and uses that make up the company's current deployment of the tech.

"There are a number of tools in use but probably the most obvious ones are Claude Code and Codex with their associated AI models," he said "They’re helping across a broad spectrum of development, with some particularly big recent wins being almost the complete elimination of non-deterministic cooking bugs which we’ve been fighting for a decade and an acceleration of work related to compressing shaders which both significantly reduce patch sizes. [Other wins include] a rewrite of a significant portion of the D3D12 rendering layer (which I estimated as needing three to six weeks of work for a single engineer, but the work was actually completed in about one week with a nice win on CPU time and fewer bugs), lots of help in keeping our internal test suites healthy as well as expanding those test suites for more coverage."

Wassmer went on to add that Fortnite's seen the additions of "automatic monitoring of PC stability", "automatic root cause analysis and automatic fix generation", which he claims have sped up the rectifying of long-running issues. He also noted that, engine-wise, Epic have been able to attempt "some larger architectural refactors with AI" than they previously could due to the amount of file changes required.

The dev went on to confirm that the Epic Store launcher preview released the other week isn't the only bit of vibe-coding the company have been up to, with the practice also being used in Unreal Engine development. "Yes, we are vibe-coding things," he said. "That means our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code, but they are still guiding the tools to get the architectural result we want. We’re not ‘one-shotting’ the engine; we’re iterating with AI to ship features developers want and keep the engine within the memory, performance, and scalability envelopes."

Wassmer also managed to fit in some justification as to why Epic see no other way forward then shoving a bunch of genAI into their development, largely parroting the typical talking point of 'everyone's going to be doing it soon and we can't possibly be seen to miss out on that gold rush for short-term speediness, baby'. "We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism," is one of the lines he actually said.

To be fair, at least Wassmer and Epic aren't hiding the fact they're embracing this stuff, as much as Timmy Sweens hates the concept of devs having to disclose their genAI use to prospective customers or users. Sometimes the desire of AI bros to shout about their use from the rooftops out of sheer marketing zeal has its positives, eh?

#3999. "Why the f**k would they add a perk like that?" - Modern Warfare 4 DMZ players are up in arms over the ability to self-revive

Modern Warfare 4's DMZ extraction shooter mode has only been out for two days - and only for those who pre-ordered the game - but already players are up in arms over a particular trait that allows competitors to revive themselves after being killed.

That trait is called Possum, and is one of the many abilities players can unlock as they level up their operators. How it works is this: if the trait is active, you're given the option, once per match, to revive yourself on command when killed. Doing so places you in a Last Stand state, and you'll need to pick yourself up from this vulnerable downed position to continue playing. All together, getting back into the firefight from dead takes around 10 uninterrupted seconds. You also lose any loot you've gathered when you revive - so you're back to square one.

It goes without saying that the ability to come back to life at all in an extraction shooter is a bold addition to DMZ. There doesn't seem to be a great way to see if a dead opponent has it, meaning every player you kill could come back for revenge later in the match when your guard is down. It doesn't take long to unlock either! If you focus your operator progression solely on the Warfighter path, Possum can be unlocked in a handful of hours. As such, it's likely someone in a DMZ match will be ready to pounce. And to say Possum is proving divisive among Call of Duty players would be an understatement.

"Possum is garbage and needs to be deleted ASAP," pdmaloney94 wrote on the DMZ subreddit. This mechanic breaks DMZ in my opinion and severely takes the stakes out of [matches]. After fully killing a team we now have to babysit their corpses until we can confirm that they returned to the lobby? Who on earth thought this was a good idea to implement into an extraction shooter?"

That sentiment was mirrored by other players too. "I just clutched a 1v3 in the underground mall, go to revive my teammate before looting anyone, and the first person I killed is laying in the corner and kills me, "SkinDiesel wrote. "Why the f**k would they add a perk like that to an extraction shooter? I get the self-revives and tourniquets, but reviving yourself from death for free every single game is diabolical."

Some players pushed back, however, offering a more measured evaluation of Possum and some strategies to counter it. "Just move on and they won’t catch you because they have no loot to pursue," suggested cleppingout. Wilus82 brought up an interesting idea too: "I was reading that people were saying to put trip mines or land mines on their bodies."

Already, prominent Call of Duty YouTubers are decrying the trait. Phixate lambasted it as "completely broken", while Wynn-Gaming called Possum "crazy" - the trait drawing criticism largely due to its potential impact on team-vs-team gunfights. After all, pushing toward a team once you take down one of their members and thin out the ranks is a strategy as old as time. If that apparent numbers advantage suddenly evaporates mid-conflict, it's potentially a big deal.

My take? I hope Possum doesn't get nerfed, at least for a few weeks. Let it ride. Already we're seeing the way it's encouraging players to adopt interesting new strategies, and two days isn't nearly enough time to determine whether the trait is genuinely broken. Let the meta game settle, allow people to push it to its limits, then, if it remains a problem by December, call pest patrol on the possum.

DMZ's new trait isn't the only thing raising eyebrows, of course.. Players have been spawning in the middle of roads and immediately getting run over, which is hilarious. It'll be interesting to see what else emerges when the wider populace gains access later today.

MachineGames is rumoured to be working on a third Wolfenstein game.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Id Software has tightened its relationship with fellow shooter specialists MachineGames according to studio co-director Marty Stratton, after Xbox laid off roughly half of the Doom developer's employees earlier this year.

Stratton was asked how the studio was doing following Xbox's massive job cuts at a recent press event for Doom: The Dark Ages' Revelations DLC (via IGN) and he was keen to assure everyone that things are hunky dory at the legendary FPS developer.

"We're doing great," Stratton explained. "Not to handwave the [layoffs] away … everybody knows we had about half of our studio exit as part of that. But there was a very deliberate effort to make sure that we were incredibly viable coming out of that across everything we do, across game development and [the] technology department."

As part of its response to those layoffs, id Software has apparently deepened its ties with MachineGames, developers of Wolfenstein: The New Order and, more recently, the excellent Indiana Jones and the Great Circle.

"We're working more closely with MachineGames than ever," Stratton said. "We've always had a very close partnership with them, but I think we're at the point with technology development that both teams are incredibly talented and have incredibly talented engineers and we're really on an amazing path that had started pre-[layoffs]. We'd kicked this off earlier this year. We're really excited about that. We're both really, really bullish on what we have ahead.

Stratton's comments have led to speculation that the two developers may be cooperating on Wolfenstein 3, which MachineGames is rumoured to be working on. Id Software has just concluded active development of Doom: The Dark Ages following the expansions' release, so this is possible. What's interesting to me, however, is how Stratton repeatedly references technology.

The id Software layoffs heavily impact the developer's Frankfurt arm, including numerous designers of the formidable id-tech engine. This led to fears that id-tech was being shelved. Microsoft contradicted this, though further reports left the question open. But Stratton's comments lead me to believe we might be seeing a tech alignment between the two developers as a result of those Frankfurt layoffs.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

While id Software built Doom: The Dark Ages on id-tech 8, MachineGames used a modified version of id-tech 7, called Motor, for Indiana Jones and the Great Circle. The fact that Stratton references both teams' "incredibly talented engineers" suggests to me that id Software is folding MachineGames' engine programmers directly into id-tech's ongoing development, with both teams working on the engine concurrently going forward. Assuming that id tech hasn't been canned outright, this approach would make sense given the expertise id Software lost from its Frankfurt arm.

Sadly, the layoffs that affected id Software were far from the last at Xbox. After cutting 1600 jobs in the summer, Xbox initiated a second wave of layoffs in September that also saw Obsidian and Bethesda merge and put Activision in charge of Halo. Further Xbox layoffs are planned leading up to January 2027, while Microsoft more broadly has offered a "voluntary exit offer" to over a quarter of its workforce.

#3997. Company of Heroes 3's Operation Torch DLC ships off to North Africa in November, for new missions based around the Allied landings

Atten-shun! Company Of Heroes 3's got new single-player missions inbound via a DLC set during the Allies' 1942 invasion of North Africa. You'll take charge of American forces through a campaign steeped in second world war history that's designed to test your tactical nous and ability to upgrade fighting units to come out on top.It's out on November 25th.

As is made rather obvious by its name, the DLC depicts Operation Torch, which saw the Brits and yanks work together to invade Vichy France-controlled Algeria and Morocco. There's a "dramatic campaign arc that spans the opening invasion, the defeat at Kasserine, and the final assault on Hill 609", no doubt with copious mentions of names like Eisenhower and Patton across its 15 missions.

You'll don the boots of three American soldiers who're either in command or in the thick of the action on the battlefield, with devs Relic noting that their "perspectives reflect the hardships, losses, responsibilities, and lessons learned as they are forged into the fighting force that will liberate Europe".

In between the likes of urban tank battles and stealth ops, you'll pick upgrades earned through completing objectives, ensuring your troops fight in the manner that best suits your preferred tactical slant. For example, I assume you'll be able to go all-in on artillery if all you're after is some big booms that look impressive, but might prove useless if the enemy are safely tucked away in deep cover waving their middle fingers at your boys.

"Company Of Heroes 3 is a rip-roaring return to form and then some for Relic's much loved RTS, and its stirring orchestral score will have you beating your chest and yelling hoo-rah like only the best toy soldier fantasies can," former RPS commander-in-chief Katharine wrote of COH 3 on release in 2023. "If Relic can iron out some of those lingering campaign niggles, this could easily be an all-timer for WWII strategy buffs."

More recently, current boss Julian gave roguelite spin-off Company of Heroes 3: Final Stand a go, coming out with the impression that it's a shakeup which succeded in increasing his appreciation for the series.

#3996. Mass Effect crossover items have seemingly been removed from Battlefield 6 following EA's sudden closure of BioWare

After EA's sudden shutdown of developer BioWare, upcoming crossover items themed around Mass Effect appear to have been removed from Battlefield 6.

When Battlefield 6's Season Five dropped earlier this month, many eager fans spotted that a collection of Mass Effect items had sneakily been added to the shooter's cosmetic menus, but were still unavailable to unlock or buy. The cosmetics included a little Normandy ship charm that dangled off weapons, some weapons that wouldn't look out of place in Mass Effect's sci-fi world and a few N7 tags. (Good spot, IGN!)

DICE has quietly removed all 'Mass Effect' cosmetics from #Battlefield6 after BioWare closure. Player card backgrounds, weapon skins, weapon charms, weapon stickers, sprays, soldier patches... everything. https://t.co/8KkjOm8nX2

With N7 Day right around the corner - slated for the 7th of November, as per usual - series fans reckoned the items would serve to celebrate the series' annual tradition and perhaps herald more news of Mass Effect 5. Those hopes were short-lived, sadly - developer BioWare is no more and the next Mass Effect game has been cancelled.

Following the shock closure, all Mass Effect items have seemingly been scrubbed from Battlefield 6's menus. Players spotted their absence in no time and shared the news online.

Battlefield 6's recent Dead Space crossover event already invited lots of divided opinions, with some players upset that the widely loved horror series is stuck in limbo while EA uses it to feed its live-service machine. Perhaps pulling a similar trick with Mass Effect - by celebrating N7 Day despite the series' uncertain future - would've simply poured salt onto a freshly opened wound. Although, the cosmetics were seemingly finished and ready to go.

In its announcement memo, EA said it was "making deliberate choices to align talent and investment where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth" - hence the decision to lay off 400 workers and cut BioWare entirely. The games industry has since mourned the loss of a beloved, long-standing role-playing institution.

A former BioWare dev recently claimed Mass Effect 5 would've borrowed from Baldur's Gate 3 and The Witcher to deliver unprecedented player choice. We'll never know for sure what BioWare would've cooked up, but a leaked trailer for Mass Effect Universe gives us a taste - a small, bittersweet, neon-drenched taste.

EA itself was recently taken private by the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund, Jared Kushner's private equity group Affinity Partners and Silver Lake in a $55bn leveraged buyout.

#3995. Petit Planet coming to Switch 2 in 2027

miHoYo will release a Switch 2 version of free-to-play cosmic life simulation game Petit Planet in 2027, the developer announced. It will launch first for PC via Epic Games Store and client download, iOS via App Store, and Android via Google Play on December 4, as previously announced.

In Petit Planet, players take on the role of Planet Tenders, journeying to the Starsea on the back of Oumuamua, a Starsea Spirit said to listen to the wishes in people’s hearts. On their very own planet, they plant a Luca Seed that gradually grows into a Luca Arbor, shaping the planet’s landscape, seasons, and ecosystem over time. Life on the planet is never lonely. Planet Coordinator Mobai and Starsea Racer Elsasani are the first to welcome each Planet Tender to their new home, with more Neighbors arriving over time, each with their own stories to tell. As players get to know their Neighbors, chance encounters can blossom into lasting friendships. Beyond life on their home planet, players can set sail across the Starsea to explore its scattered Islets, or head to the Galactic Bazaar to enjoy games, take part in auctions, and share their creations.

To celebrate the upcoming launch, HoYoverse has prepared a series of events and rewards for Planet Tenders. A pre-registration lucky draw on the official website offers exciting prizes, while over 1,000 clothing and furniture items can be earned for free through regular gameplay. In the “Besties, Made to Match!” event, players who team up with two friends to pre-register will each receive an exclusive clothing item. Starting November 1, the special “Launch a Planet” event invites players to design their own planets on the official event website, with a chance to win surprise grand prizes. The first Petit Planet Seasonal Creation Event will kick off alongside the game’s launch, offering cash prizes, in-game rewards, and official merchandise for selected fan creations. After the special program, players can also visit Petit Planet‘s official X account to receive a “Moving Guide” and enter for a chance to win a suitcase, gift cards, and an exclusive luggage tag.

It seems rumors that Sam Houser is just a "taste director" are bunk

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rockstar's notoriously private co-founder and president, Sam Houser, hasn't said a whole lot in public about his involvement in the studio's forthcoming behemoth, GTA 6, leading to a fair degree of rumor and speculation that he's taken a backseat in the actual day-to-day creative decision-making. That is not true in the slightest, according to Rockstar North co-studio head and head of development, Rob Nelson.

Talking to Edge for its big GTA 6 cover story, Nelson put the idea of Houser being little more than a "taste director" ala record producer Rick Rubin to bed. Nelson's exact words are paraphrased by Edge's editors, but Nelson insists that Houser was involved with the initial conception and general direction of GTA 6 and that he's integrally linked to every aspect of the game's creative direction, dispelling any suggestion that he's simply overseeing the company and general vibe of the project without as much direct creative input as earlier GTA games.

"Sam and I will identify problems or issues that we then solve with and across the teams," says Nelson of Houser's involvement. Nelson also says he spends a couple of weeks with Houser every time there's a new milestone in GTA 6's development, and together they come up with feedback addressing nitty gritty stuff like lighting and audio to more fundamental issues involving game mechanics, tone, and narrative. The feedback is then sent to the relevant teams, who work through Nelson and Houser's list of issues before the process picks back up again.

Of course, with a map size rivaling GTA 4, GTA 5, and Red Dead Redemption 2 combined, and a world where "you can go anywhere, any random location, and so many people have thought about that location," there's no way any one person can have eyes on every single tiny little detail in the game, but it's clear that Houser remains a foundational creative influence in the GTA canon even more than 30 years later.

#3993. Cyberpunk trading sim Probably Stolen is about running a kiosk in a space station full of gangs, megacorps, and secret rogue cyborgs

I will have you know this is an original Malorian Arms 3516

I have so far not been shivved, shanked, brain fried, hazed, wasted, ironed, short-circed, flat-lined or even complained at in Probably Stolen - Cyberpunk Shopkeeper Sim, but I'm sure it's just a matter of time.

In this neuromantic kiosk game from Questing Goose Studio, you're a new store owner aboard a backwater space station. Each day, you roll up the shutter and do business with a procession of shady types, ranging from janitors with unappetising beards to sexy cowled folk with Main Character tattoos. The basics are simple enough, for all the overwhelmingly menu-led presentation: buy what you can afford, according to your instinct for the wider market, sell what you can fit into the customer's budget. But things quickly get complicated.

You've got to watch out for wanted criminals, checking them against mugshots and possibly, reporting them to security. You've got to think about how your transactions shape the opinions of various factions, from revolutionaries through corpo bosses to the mob. You've got to run a magnifying glass over robot hands and cigarette packets, identifying vintage pieces and counterfeits. You've got to head out at night to scrounge stock from the dumps, preferably without getting shivved, shanked, etcetera. You've got to pay the electricity bill. You've got to shoot rogue androids in the CPU.

I've only peeked timidly over the counter of Probably Stolen, which I would cautiously characterise as Papers, Please with a lot more wheeling and dealing, but it feels like there's some decent substance here. I'm particularly intrigued by the idea of diversifying my operations beyond bog-standard checkout work.

"Start as a gunsmith, chemist, water merchant, fence, farmer, or from absolute rock bottom," the Steam page growls. "Every product line has its own profit curve and its own way of ruining you, weapons bring inspections, chemicals bring addiction, water brings liability, contraband brings raids. Some trades need heavy machinery and permits, others just a good hiding spot and a straight face. The better the margins, the worse the consequences when something goes wrong. You’re not choosing a theme for your shop, you’re choosing which kind of trouble you’re willing to monetize."

Oof! I'll use that closing line next time I interview a producer about season passes. Maybe I'll use it next time I have to pick a wallpaper pattern for my flat.

As cyberpunk fictions go, this does seem very comfortable. Your store has a cassette player with a selection of synthy music - I turned it off after 30 seconds, because the tunes were so gratingly generic. Dare I say it, cyberpunk is a "cosy" genre these days, but perhaps I just need to trade up to some classier earworms.

I also don't think much of Probably Stolen's writing, which seems clipped and flavourless, but it's getting the job done, and besides, I'm very early on in my career as a skanky pawnshop operator. I haven't even sold any toilet roll yet, and that feels like the real rite of passage. People who prefer their Netrunner 7-Elevens all 3D and hung with beautiful, beautiful birdcages might prefer the dives you get in No Law, which Julian saw recently.

#3992. As devastating Xbox "reset" continues, Dishonored studio Arkane Lyon reportedly only has until November to find a new buyer before it's closed

After getting caught up in Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's devastating layoffs and cuts earlier this year, Arkane Lyon - the beloved immersive sim studio behind the likes of Dishonored and Deathloop - reportedly only has until November to find a buyer. If the search fails, it will be shut down.

Arkane Lyon was one of a number of first-party studios reportedly facing closure ahead of Xbox's massive "reset" in July. However, when the layoffs were officially announced - bringing confirmation that 3,200 Xbox employees will eventually lose their jobs as part of the sweeping restructuring - Microsoft revealed Psychonauts developer Double Fine, State of Decay studio Undead Labs, and South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games would go independent following negotiations.

Hellblade studio Ninja Theory is now likely to close after two acquisition deals fell through, only leaving the fate of Arkane Lyon - a studio Microsoft acquired in 2021 when it purchased ZeniMax - uncertain. At the time, Xbox said it was "beginning required consultation with its Works Council to review potential strategic options" regarding Arkane, but little has been heard since.

Now, a report by French publication Le Monde (via Google Translate) has shed additional light on the studio's fate. Speaking to the publication, Printemps Écologique and the Video Game Workers’ Union (STJV) said Xbox management had informed Arkane Lyon it was facing closure on 16th July. As Le Monde notes, however, Microsoft's plan was complicated by French law, which requires a company with more than 1,000 employees to spend three months seeking a new buyer for any operational arm it plans to close. Only then, if no buyer is found, can it be shut down.

According to Le Monde, the search - alongside a consultation process and negotiations regarding an employment protection plan - began this summer, and the deadline to find a buyer for the studio is imminent, ending on 13th November. If the closure occurs, 217 workers could lose their jobs.

However, a union representative told the publication redundancy negotiations, which seemingly include efforts to get Arkane workers redeployed to other Microsoft studios, are going "badly", and that unions are trying to buy more time in the hope of saving the studio and its jobs. Reportedly, "several forms of takeover are being considered."

In response to the report, Microsoft did not confirm or deny Arkane's proposed closure, but told Le Monde, "We continue to explore various options for Arkane as part of the ongoing French consultation process". It also said it was "keeping the Social and Economic Committee and our employees informed." Internal documents seen by the publication say "the implementation of the plan [for the total and definitive cessation of the company's operations] is scheduled to begin at the end of 2026 and is expected to continue throughout the first quarter of 2027."

Amid all this turmoil, it's unclear what might happen to Arkane Lyon's current project, Marvel's Blade. In July, Xbox insisted "none of [its] first-party publicly announced games or projects" would be cancelled as part of Sharma's cuts, suggesting Blade - which hasn't been seen since its announcement in 2023 - was safe. Earlier this year, the game was rumoured to be dead, but a follow-up report from The Verge claimed that while it was "over-budget", it was now targeting a release in 2027 after an internal delay.

Earlier this month, Sharma insisted Xbox had "started to return to growth" following the company's sweeping cuts, but reports suggest three more rounds of layoffs are still to come, possibly starting before October is through.

Funcom will also "continue expanding the game" through 2027.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Thus far, Funcom has focussed mainly on changes to its survival MMO Dune: Awakening, with the Norwegian studio reworking the entire game to function as both a solo experience and a PvE adventure. Now that overhaul is done, however, Funcom is now set on expanding players' adventures on Arrakis, having just announced a free expansion that adds a new and completely different map to explore.

Coming in December, the Blood and Ice DLC will let players depart the searing sands of Arrakis for the planet's frozen north, adding a new survival map called the Polar Sink that flips the game's central survival concept on its head. Rather than avoiding the heat, players will actively have to seek it out, while also developing new technologies to help them adapt to the extreme change in climate.

There's some variance within this environment too. The Polar Sink is composed of two different biomes, the tundra and the icecap. While the icecap is the more extreme of the two, both areas are closely guarded by "water shippers", wealthy traders who supply Arrakis' second most-valuable resource from the polar regions down to the deserts. Players' primary objective in the DLC will be breaking the water shippers' stranglehold on the ice, which they can then use to cool their base equipment back in the desert and speed up resource production.

Funcom says that the expansion adds "around 35 hours of new progression", which sounds pretty beefy for a free DLC. It also apparently "brings the focus back to ground-level survival" for veteran players, "traversal, temperature management and combat all playing important roles in your progression."

Blood and Ice will be released on December 1. Alongside the expansion, Funcom has also introduced a Cosmetics Store to Awakening, and is also working on several other heavily requested features. These include an offline single-player mode that's coming in November (the game can be played solo right now, but only with an Internet connection) and fully supported cross-play in January next year.

Funcom also says that Blood and Ice represents "another step in the ongoing development of Dune: Awakening" and that it will "continue expanding the game" through 2027. This falls in line with the studio's recent announcement that it was pivoting to exclusively support its existing games—which includes Conan Exiles alongside Dune: Awakening—and was laying off an unspecified number of employees as a result of that shift in strategy.

#3990. GTA 6 has a smell reaction system, which immediately joins Red Dead Redemption 2's dynamically shrinking horse balls on Rockstar's list of immersive symbols of excess

Florida of course being full of smelly smells that smell...smelly

Any reminder of Red Dead Redemption 2's temperature sensitive horse testicles brings a smile to my face. In truth, I can't say I've ever zoomed in close enough to properly take in the spectacle of Arthur Morgan's mount having its nuts dynamically expand and contract based on whether he's riding through snowy mountains or across baking plains, but I do always get a kick out of knowing such a thing's happening as I play. To this point, the horse balls have been the most infamous or meme-worthy example of Rockstar's obsession with going all-in on realistic detail to an arguably unnecessary degree, one that borders on overindulgence which players could conceivably never notice if they weren't expressly told about it.

That philosophy's gone nowhere, so GTA 6 was always going to have a feature that'd become as much of a metaphor for excess as those beloved balls. It may well be the smell reaction system revealed in Edge's long read on the game.

According to this latest rundown of things in GTA 6 and how they were made, Rockstar devs at one point had to make a character react to a not nice smell for a specific bit of "explorable content" stuffed into the game. Cool. One person scrunching their face up to show things are getting stinky in one minigame or mission. Leave it at that.

They reportedly did not leave it at that, later going back to flesh out this one smell reaction into a broader system which other locations to inspire various degrees of face-scrunching by protagonists Lucia and Jason. Cue, in the demo of the game in action which Rockstar gave Edge, Jason walking into a house and starting to act like someone who's just walked into a shower-averse teenager's bedroom during a heatwave despite that not having been set up as part of a deliberately crafted encounter. It's horse ball-esque dynamic systems playing off each other, and voila, a man going eewwwwwwwwwwwww.

Would GTA 6 be any worse off if, as in previous entries, you weren't being shown as expressly which places the crim whose boots you're sharing finds a bit too pongy for their liking? Almost certainly not, but hey, when you've decided your business is taking the detail to levels other games could only dream of having the budget for, getting to the point where you're adding a fiftieth layer of icing to a cake so packed to the gills with different tastes and flourishes that your guests will struggle to appreciate or even notice them all unless you painstakingly point out each one is sort of inevitable.

Another layer of gold wrap on the Bugatti, another brick made of diamonds in a wall projected to be the most lucrative of all time, another farty stench in a room already drowning in foul aromas. It's beautiful in the perverse sort of way that I imagine the Palace of Versailles was to anyone who wandered its gilded halls just prior to the French revolution. To be clear, this isn't any sort of slight on the devs who'll no doubt have worked hard to bring this system and others in GTA 6 to life, a number of whom have a recoginition vote on their unionisation efforts coming up next month.

From a player perspective, one can only hope that by the time GTA 6 hits PC, the RAM crisis has led hardware makers to invest heavily in smellivision tech, so that players around the world can drink in the guffs causing their butt naked on-screen analogue's eyes to water or revel in the stink caused by hitting someone with a bag of dog shit. Forget AI bollocks, this is the future, I scream as I retch into a toilet bowl while some funky tunes from Justice play in the background.

#3989. With Minecraft and Diablo shows already on the way, Netflix reportedly offered Xbox $500m for a bigger film and TV deal

A deal between Netflix and Xbox has supposedly fallen through because of one minor quibble: Netflix wanted to adapt the console maker's games for $500m, not $800m.

That's according to Puck News' Matt Belloni, who reports that Netflix offered Xbox $500m to exclusively licence the company's games and turn them into streamable films or TV shows for the next seven years.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma and the division's business affairs team then responded with an eye-watering counter offer, according to the report. Xbox supposedly asked the streamer for $800m to sign off on the same deal.

Former Netflix CCO Bela Bajaria reportedly approached the game publisher first, but the executive's departure and Xbox's expensive counter offer led to the deal falling apart. Netflix CFO Spence Neumann was apparently one of the streamer's top heads who thought the deal wasn't worth the $800m price tag.

It's unclear which games would've been included in the film and TV deal considering multiple Xbox brands are already on their way to screens both big and small. Amazon is working to adapt Wolfenstein into a live-action series and will soon debut the third season of its acclaimed Fallout show, for example, while Paramount is turning Call of Duty into a blockbuster movie.

Netflix and Xbox are still working together on other projects, though. Animated shows based on Minecraft and Diablo are already in the works, as is a live-action Gears of War film. Blizzard Entertainment president Johanna Faries recently teased the crowd at BlizzCon 2026 by suggesting Overwatch and Warcraft could receive a similar treatment, too.

"We have received record-breaking interest in our IP," Xbox said in a statement to Puck News. "Netflix is a valued partner and we are excited for the forthcoming release of our Minecraft and Diablo animated series together, among other adaptations." The outlet claims Xbox is continuing to pursue smaller licensing deals.

Game adaptations are all the rage right now. This year's excellent Resident Evil reboot, Illuminations' Super Mario Bros duology, HBO's The Last of US, Amazon's Fallout and three live-action Sonic The Hedgehog films have found huge success - and encouraged practically every major studio to go hunting for their own game licenses. They're not all hits, however. This year's Street Fighter and Mortal Kombat 2 were released to a more tepid crowd.

Nicholas Hoult says his How to Rob a Bank vigilante character and DC villain Lex Luthor have a lot more in common than you'd think.

"For both of them, I think there's this element of, like, the end goal," Hoult tells GamesRadar+, when asked how Ryan and Lex Luthor compare. "They got so fixated on it. And that was what was really interesting about playing Luthor in Man of Tomorrow – I don't want to give too much away about the movie – but how James Gunn has written the character. There's a lot for Lex to try and understand about himself and the world. And so that was interesting to play."

In How to Rob a Bank, Hoult plays Ryan, the leader of a group of masked vigilantes (played by Pete Davidson, Anna Sawai, and Rhenzy Feliz) who are social media famous for their elaborate bank-robbing schemes. Ryan, either via YouTube video or livestream, gives pretty thorough instructions on how to rob a bank, evade police, and a plethora of other illegal activities. The key difference between Ryan and Lex Luthor, however, is that Ryan is doing it for the greater good. Lex, as we saw in James Gunn's Superman, is a bit more self-involved...

Continues Hoult: "But I think it's fun to play characters that have got, like, this set goal and obsession because then it gives you a very clear path through the story and the scenes."

Man of Tomorrow sees Superman and Lex Luthor come together in order to defeat Braniac, a supervillain that the Man of Steel can't take on alone. Star Nathan Fillion previously said we’ll "learn more about who Lex Luthor is" in the upcoming DC sequel.

How to Rob a Bank hits theaters on November 13. Man of Tomorrow is out July 9, 2027. For more, check out our breakdown of all the upcoming DC movies and shows on the way in 2026 and beyond.

#3986. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 intro cinematic is "not intended to reference or trivialise" real-world South Korean crowd crush, Activision say amid reported backlash

Update: Activision reportedly confirm footage will be removed in November Modern Warfare 4 update

Update: The BBC report that Activision have issued a statement apologising to the victims of the Itaewon crowd crush and confirmed that the news footage from the disaster in Modern Warfare 4's intro cinematic will be removed. An update coming to the shooter on November 12th will do the deed.

The 10.29 Itaewon Disaster Bereaved Families Association have welcomed Activision's decision to pull the footage, according to the BBC, but also said they hadn't received a direct apology from the Call of Duty publishers.

The intro cinematic of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, this year's Activision mil-shooter, has reportedly caused controversy in South Korea due to the use of some real world news footage from a 2022 crowd crush in Seoul's Itaewon district which killed around 150 people. Activision have now issued a response to the situation, in which they state the intro is "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy".

Korean site SBS News have reported on the backlash Modern Warfare 4's opening cinematic has caused in the country. Their story - which it's worth noting has been translated into English by AI, and thus is acknowledged as potentially containing errors - claimed that the shooter's intro features three seconds of real-world broadcast footage showing a emergency workers performing CPR on a collapsed person during the Itaewon crowd crush's aftermath.

The crush saw a crowd of people become trapped in a narrow alleyway during Halloween weekend celebrations in the South Korean capital, with between 150 and 160 people dying as a result of becoming so tightly packed together that some couldn't breathe. According to the report, groups and bodies in Korea including an association representing families who suffered bereavements in the crush have called for Activision to remove the footage from Modern Warfare 4's intro.

#3985. Nintendo's Shigeru Miyamoto says even if gen-AI "were to eventually handle everything, there will always be a role left" for human designers

Legendary Nintendo developer Shigeru Miyamoto - who led development on classic games such as Super Mario 64 and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time - has argued that the rise of generative AI tools won't necessarily replace human talent.

Next month, Shigeru Miyamoto will become the first ever video game developer to be awarded the Order of Culture by the Emperor of Japan, a hugely prestigious honour. But in a recent press conference dedicated to the award, he also shared some thoughts about gen-AI and its use in game production.

"Our generation lived through a period of rapid computer development - a time when tools were constantly evolving, moving from typewriters to word processors,” he said while speaking to the press, in quotes translated by VGC. Miyamoto argued that a designer's true capabilities "finally came to the fore" as technology advanced and was capable of handling more of what might be considered "labor", and a similar transition may take place with generative AI tech.

"While the act of creation is inherently satisfying, there's a danger: one might find satisfaction in the labor itself and mistakenly believe that a high-quality piece of work has been created," he added. If generative-AI software replaces more tasks involved in game production, human game devs might have "an opportunity to reflect on what's really important."

"Looking back at past designs, there are some that were created merely by copying and pasting. Yet, such work rarely stands the test of time; it lacks the individual’s particular design intention," Miyamoto continued. "Because the process relies on an individual's intent, with the computer serving as an assistant for the labor, I believe that even as technology continues to evolve, and even if AI were to eventually handle everything, there will always be a role left for us to play."

Masahiro Sakurai was a bit less optimistic about a potentially AI-first future than his peer. The Smash Bros. director recently said gen-AI tech might lead to a surge of unoriginal and unprofitable games, though it won't be able to replicate the creativity of humans.

Nintendo itself hasn't outright ruled out the possibility of using gen-AI tools in the future, but former Nintendo of America president Doug Bowser assured folks that the company's games would retain a "human touch" last year. "We still believe that what makes our games special is our developers, their artistic capabilities, their insight into how people play," Bowser said at the time.

Nintendo is somewhat at odds with several of its contemporaries when it comes to AI adoption, however. Square Enix CEO Takashi Kiryu previously said the company would be "aggressive in applying AI." Sega, Capcom, Level-5, Epic Games and a number of other high-profile game studios have admitted to using gen-AI in some form, as well. Xbox even opened an entire division seemingly dedicated to experimenting with the tech.

"Players want to feel like they're powerful and can do something cool."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Weird Weekend is our regular Saturday column where we celebrate PC gaming oddities: peculiar games, strange bits of trivia, forgotten history. Pop back every weekend to find out what Jeremy, Josh, Rick and Ted have become obsessed with this time, whether it's the canon height of Thief's Garrett or that time someone in the Vatican pirated Football Manager.

If you've played an extraction shooter like Arc Raiders or Marathon, you've probably experienced the agony of trusting another player only for them to shoot you in the head and nick all your stuff. Whenever that happens—and it's happened to me more than I'd like to admit—the same questions run through my head (after the traditional wailing and gnashing of teeth). Was that always going to happen? Did I do something wrong? Should I have said something different? Behaved differently? Or should I have simply foregone any attempt at diplomacy and shot first?

I've often wondered if there's a way to get better at this. Not just to convince other players that I'm not a threat, but to make them not want to shoot me. Conveniently, I recently had the chance to speak to someone who knows a thing or two about resolving such situations, both in videogames and real life.

James 'Pigeon' Fielder is one of only two political scientists in the world who specialise in gaming. Or at least, if there are more than two, Fielder is yet to be made aware of them: "When I talk about my research with fellow political scientists they either look at me like I'm crazy or they go 'Oh, that sounds cool.'"

Political science is the study of governments, which in turns means it's the study of human behaviour at a large-scale, organised level. Areas of interest include policy development, power distribution, and most importantly for us, conflict resolution.

What relevance does this have to games? Fielder answers this himself: "It's almost like taking theories of political science and doing fruit fly experiments, like trying to understand human behaviour, specifically human political behaviour, inside of game worlds," he says. "In a space like EVE Online, we might see political phenomena develop in weeks, months, or years that in real life would take decades or centuries to express themselves."

How does one become a political scientist specialising in games? Well, it's not exactly a job with an established career path, but Fielder arrived at it through his career in the US military, where his lifelong love of TTRPGs resulted in an aptitude for designing wargames. "I was getting groomed to be promoted from specialist to sergeant, and to be promoted, I had to demonstrate that I could teach a class," he says. "So I decided to build a class on a task that integrated roleplaying game elements. Why it seemed like a good idea at the time, I can't recall. All I know is that everybody had a great time."

Fielder's commanding officers took notice: "Once you get that stink on you in the military, like 'Oh Fielder, can you build another exercise for us?' You build another exercise, and they would get bigger and bigger," he says. "To date, the biggest exercise I've ever designed was for 5,000 people that ran 168 hours."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Fielder eventually switched from the US Army to the US Air Force and was hired by the Air Force Academy to teach political science. "My degrees are in history and national security … but it was political science who hired me." During a lesson on social capital or "why do people trust each other" as Fielder puts it, one student asked a question—can people develop trust in online games the same way they do in person?

"Like a good scientist, I went 'Huh, I don't know. Let me look that up," Fielder says. "That's when I started learning why games are so effective at bringing people together."

To very briefly summarise why games are effective in this manner: while the scenarios games present are fictional, the feelings they produce in the people playing them are very real. Anyone who has rage-quit a game will understand this. But games are also capable of producing more complex emotions and imagined states of being.

With roleplaying games in particular, they encourage people to inhabit personalities and mental states other than their own. In the right circumstances, these feelings can help instil empathy or new perspectives in people. "A [prison] inmate, for example, might put on the character of a lawful good hero," Fielder posits. "Now, when I'm supposed to be stealing from people, or using violence or vandalism, I'm going to play a Paladin, and now I'm inculcating what it's like to be a lawful good Paladin. I get debriefed at the end of the game, and I go 'Oh, it actually felt good. It felt good to be playing that different person.'"

Fielder has applied these techniques in a military context, such as forecasting the outcome of elections in Afghanistan as he discussed in a 2023 TeDX talk. But since retiring from the military, he's also applied these techniques in a civilian context, running games and exercises for businesses, prisons, and other institutions.

What's especially interesting, though, is that the lessons learned from playing out scenarios in the real world can then feed back into games and game design. To take the latter first, alongside his political science work, Fielder is also an RPG designer and design consultant: "When I run games at conventions and I run one shots, if it's an invention that I've designed, I work to try to maximise the amount of agency players have," he says.

"Players want to feel like they're powerful and can do something cool, even if it's an unforgiving setting like Call of Cthulhu …. Where the lethality is high, players like to think that the decisions they make matter, and when they do, when the dice work against them and they can see the dice fall, they're more likely to accept it as fair."

Likewise, players can deploy techniques for deescalation and establishing trust used in the real world in games too, which is where we circle back to extraction shooters. Fielder starts by pointing out that the rules of the game must support cooperation to begin with. "If it's a game like the original iteration of PUBG, then that's impossible because you know that 'The only way to win is I have to kill everybody.'"

This might seem obvious. But it's also applicable on a sliding scale—the more explicit and involved the rules are for cooperation, the more likely players will use them. This is why you're more likely to see cooperation in Arc Raiders than Marathon. While Marathon has the capacity for cooperative play, this idea hasn't filtered through to the playerbase in the way it did with Arc Raiders, perhaps because of its faster TTK, or its friendly callout being less clear than Arc Raiders' 'Don't Shoot!'

But assuming that the rules apply and there's at least a base level of comprehension. "The best way—it's not foolproof—is to approach without visible weapons. If there's a way to have an emoticon where you can have your hands outstretched … and this comes from my military background, [it] demonstrates 'Look, my hands are empty, and it's very difficult for me to grab a weapon, even in a videogame.'"

In addition, Fielder says trust is established a lot faster if you have something to offer and offer it freely. "I don't expect anything in return except let's not fight," he says. "The more valuable that item is, the more receptive your audience will be." He concedes that there is a risk here. "If you offer something very valuable they [might] go, 'Oh, maybe he has more stuff.'"

Fielder has spent much of his life studying and using games as a method to resolve conflict. But there is one area of conflict where a solution still eludes him, and that's within the gaming community itself. "It actually hurts me when I see social differences in the gaming space, gatekeepers over racial differences, gender differences, or players [who] are angered with each other," he says.

"In reality, one of the best places to overcome differences with people is a game. You learn, you sit down to play, you work together to overcome an objective," Fielder continues. "Gaming should be the most inclusive space in the world. And why it's not always that case, I don't know."

Rick has been fascinated by PC gaming since he was seven years old, when he used to sneak into his dad's home office for covert sessions of Doom. He grew up on a diet of similarly unsuitable games, with favourites including Quake, Thief, Half-Life and Deus Ex. Between 2013 and 2022, Rick was games editor of Custom PC magazine and associated website bit-tech.net. But he's always kept one foot in freelance games journalism, writing for publications like Edge, Eurogamer, the Guardian and, naturally, PC Gamer. While he'll play anything that can be controlled with a keyboard and mouse, he has a particular passion for first-person shooters and immersive sims.

#3983. Xbox's first chief operating officer Helen Chiang leaves Microsoft just three months into the job

UPDATE: Xbox responds, and source familiar with the situation alleges Chiang was terminated for "policy violations".

UPDATE 6.00pm (UK): In a formal statement, Xbox told Eurogamer: "We don't discuss individual personnel matters. We're grateful for Helen's years of service and wish her well".

A verified source familiar with the situation separately told Eurogamer that Helen Chiang had allegedly been "terminated for policy violations". Eurogamer has not been able to independently verify this claim.

Eurogamer has contacted Helen Chiang for comment.

ORIGINAL STORY 2.00pm BST: Helen Chiang, Xbox's first-ever chief operating officer (COO), is leaving Microsoft just three months after taking the job.

According to The Verge, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma confirmed Chiang's departure in an internal memo circulated on 23rd October.

"Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today. I'm grateful for her years of service and wish her well," Sharma wrote.

Sharma provided no details on why Chiang - who'd been at Microsoft for 21 years and had previously served as head of Minecraft - was leaving the company, only adding, "we'll share more on COO leadership as plans are finalised". It's thought her duties will be shared between other Xbox execs.

Sharma created the role in July as part of Xbox's massive "reset", saying it was needed to "work toward a shared goal, make the right tradeoffs, and get things done". It also came with 3200 layoffs and four studio departures in "most significant" Xbox restructuring in history.

Microsoft revealed that Psychonauts developer Double Fine, State of Decay studio Undead Labs, and South of Midnight developer Compulsion Games would go independent following negotiations, while Hellblade developer Ninja Theory is now likely to close after two acquisition deals fell through.

Arkane Lyon - the beloved immersive sim studio behind the likes of Dishonored and Deathloop - is the one still in limbo, and yesterday we learned it reportedly only has until November to find a buyer.

#3982. Can the SideWinder Game Pad, Microsoft's first game controller, work on modern PCs? I bought three of them to find out

The past and fiddly present of the Xbox controller's ancestor

1996 gave us two incredible gifts. The first was me. The second, arguably more impactful on the course of human civilisation, was the Microsoft SideWinder Game Pad 1.0.

Chances are you might not have heard of the SideWinder brand. Launched in 1995 with the 3D Pro and Standard joysticks, the hardware family would eventually comprise gamepads, racing wheels, a game voice device to talk with friends and vocally control your game, and a massive mouse with more buttons than my nana’s vest. A genuinely cool collection of peripherals.

However, and perhaps prophetic of how they would eventually set about dismantling a gaming industry they had helped built, Microsoft shuttered the SideWinder brand in 2003, supposedly due to poor sales. An especially funny comment, in hindsight, came from Microsoft Canada’s then marketing manager, Kim McWhinnie:

"While SideWinder devices are very popular, the majority of PC games today are built for a mouse and keyboard interface.”

Well before the yacht-printing success of the Steam Deck and handheld PC gaming, a significant chunk of PC players have long preferred the feel and functionality of a controller. Although the SideWinder name enjoyed a brief resurrection in 2007 with the release of the SideWinder Mouse, and later the SideWinder X6 and X4 keyboards, the gamepad side of the brand would never again see another product, with Microsoft instead opting for PC-compatible versions of their Xbox controllers.

Which bring us to 2026. While making my weekly car boot excursion, the fates conspired to bring me and the SideWinder Game Pad 1.0 together, in the form of a nice old lady asking for 2 euros. Bonafide hardware history, for that little cash? I was sold, and determined to see how a controller from the 90s might stand up to PCs and games of the 21st century.

Sadly, the initial feel of the controller isn’t great. The shell is cut from cheap plastic that sits awkwardly in my hands. Rather than a thumbstick, the controller boasts this odd circular D-Pad that allows for eight directional movement, though the diagonals are notably harder to press. The triggers give a nice clicking sound, but they feel far too thin to enjoy pushing down. The buttons are fine, though the press is much too soft for my thumb-tastes.

The controller does appear to have built with the idea of 'serious gaming' in mind. For instance, the pad comes bundled with software allowing for the creation of macros that can then be deployed at the push of the big M on the controller. Other interesting details include the early design choices that would eventually be mimicked on the first Xbox controller, the "Duke". The omni-directional D-Pad and the triple button rows make their debut here, though the size of the controller is much more in line with the later "Controller S" model, which shed much of the Duke’s girth.

The SideWinder also came with a rather neat 'pass through' port, allowing owners to connect additional SideWinder controllers through the initial controller, daisy chaining up to a total of four. Sadly, I lacked the friends necessary to examine this aspect, so you’ll have to make do with the purely imaginary scenario of securing victory by pulling on your controller hard enough to yank everyone else’s to the ground. Which, if nothing else, shows Microsoft really understood their target audience.

There's no denying the power of old controllers to provoke fond memories in the handler, nor their continued popularity in the modern day - as evident in Nintendo's production of imitation Gamecube and NES pads for the Switch 2. With growing preferences for emulation in the face of bankrupting retro game prices, many either go for custom controllers with modern functionality, or original peripherals connected via adapters, in order to preserve as much of the original experience as possible. But can the same be said for the SideWinder?

While I tracked down an old TV ad for the controller, my trawling of numerous old gaming magazines was less fruitful. I did come across a glowing review from the November 1996 issue of PC Zone by Dave Mathelson, praising the "two clever underneath buttons" (triggers were, indeed, a novelty at the time) and describing the handles as "horns" and the general design, more concerning, as "sexy". The verdict was almost entirely positive, praising both the feel and the ability to create custom control schemes for each of your games. Yet, I feel this line perhaps betrays the controller's struggles:

"While there are plenty of pads now available for the PC, the number of joysticks on the market didn't stop Microsoft from releasing one..."

As much as I find the SideWinder interesting, I'd argue it's more generic-looking than sexy. The late 90s/early 00s gave us attitude, explosions, and impractical designs you could only get by locking up a bunch of coked-up mandrills with CAD modelling software. An era ruled by the SpaceOrb 360 and the Fragmaster, the kind of creations birthed by an out-of-touch executive demanding kung-fu grip. Even Microsoft's own SideWinder Strategic Commander, an early attempt at an RTS mouse, had that strangeness sauce.

By comparison, the SideWinder Game Pad cuts a very subtle figure. There’s a seriousness to it. Still playful, as we are dealing with gaming. The nerd equivalent of dressing up in a new suit but leaving the top button undone. It feels like they were going for something more professional. The macro feature and the ability to customise your controller scheme for each game accentuate this point further, while also showcasing a design ethos Microsoft have long since abandoned: trusting consumers with the product you sold them.

Yet this also means it doesn’t stand out. I think Microsoft must have realised this at some point, as later additions to the SideWinder brand are more distinct, both visually and functionally. The Force Feedback Pro went on to sell over a million units, but the Game Pad hardly gets a mention in the news archives. For every Reddit post or TikTok short or LGR Review on weird and wonderful tech, the bland 1.0 is memory-holed even deeper.

Then, of course, there’s one other serious issue that keeps the SideWinder buried in the cable bin of yesterday: modern compatability.

As you can imagine, these things aren’t exactly easy to get working on a present-day PC.

My desktop, despite being a little dated itself, lacked the necessary connections to test the SideWinder. My motherboard still boasts old-school PS2 connectors for keyboard and mouse, but couldn’t spare a thought for more specialised retro gear. Granted, it’s not hard to see why. The controller (and a lot of the tech from the era) makes use of a 15-pin game port connector, appearing first on dedicated PCI cards, then later sound cards and eventually motherboards. These would eventually be phased out as USB became the go-to connector for personal computers, and while game port-to-USB adapters do exist, and even come bundled with later SideWinder products, procuring one today is surprisingly difficult.

So I went for the next best thing: a sound card from the 90s. A Creative Sound Blaster Live, torn from some ancient machine to grace me with the soft beauty of 16-bit audio and the game port’s connective tissue. I then quickly discovered that the card wasn’t compatible with my motherboard. Growing desperate as I battled both a looming deadline and my partner’s concern at the growing horde of retro tech, I managed to find someone selling two more SideWinders AND the game port-to-USB adapter. I snapped them up, plugged the adapter into my system, aaaaaand...

Nothing. The computer just couldn’t find it.

I’m saddened to admit I still attempted to get the blasted thing working long after this, eventually culminating in injuring myself while attempting to plant the sound card in an older machine. Taking this as a sign from the tech gods that I was not truly worthy of enjoying this artifact, I instead settled for a slightly newer (albeit still ancient) SideWinder Plug and Play. This came with USB out of the box, at the cost of fewer buttons and even less individuality, but I felt it would serve to at least give you some idea of how a SideWinder controller plays. Rest assured that if you think this damages the integrity of this retrospective, there is no one more ashamed than myself.

Prior to writing the article, I had a chat with my dad regarding the SideWinder Game Pad. He couldn’t stop gushing about it, saying how it was one of his favourite controllers back in the day. Unlike with Father Christmas, it appears my dad was telling the truth. The Plug and Play was genuinely fun to use, though perhaps not for the reasons my dad would expect.

I immediately fired up a multiplayer lobby of Titanfall 2, an FPS defined by its intricate movement systems, and proceeded to patiently stroll down the city streets, gaze locked forward. I could neither sprint nor turn the camera. In addition, incomplete control mapping also meant I couldn’t even shoot. I nearly fell out of my chair laughing as I was absolutely and immediately demolished.

I gave the original, 1993 Doom a whirl next, though again faced the issue of needing to dual wield with my PC mouse to rotate the camera for effective demon slaying. I ended up crab-walking into rooms, running back out, and letting the enemies funnel into my view. So somewhat more successful here.

Continuing my testing through retro and modern alike, I unleashed eco justice with Cloud in the original Final Fantasy VII, went bust in a round of Balatro, and tended to my farm in Stardew Valley. The SideWinder held up in all of them. I also gave some upcoming indie demos a whirl, successfully battling a demonic incursion in Entropy but tragically getting torn apart by bugs in The Last Exterminator.

Overall, so long as your game doesn’t require too many inputs (and also ideally takes place entirely within a straight hallway), the controller works great. My verdict? Ideal for Deep Space Corridor.

I'm sure that the SideWinder Game Pad 1.0 can be made to work with modern systems. Given enough time and a few more blows to my bank account, I could either fit my computer with the correct hardware, or hack together a game port adapter with an Arduino board.

I don’t intend to give up, but it’s also a pain point that’s going to be too much for a lot of people. Tech continues to hurtle forward, abandoning anything deemed inefficient for the world of tomorrow, with little care for ensuring compatabiltiy with the successes of yesterday. Sony already showed as much with their promise/threat to ditch physical games media. Do you think Microsoft are going to care about a controller that Asha Sharma has probably never heard of, much less used?

The truth of the matter is that, as foundational as the tech is, the SideWinder Game Pad was just an early casualty in an arms race that has slowly stripped uniqueness, choice, and especially this past year, affordability from players. Give it another decade, and if the tech overlords have their way, we’ll likely be renting our machines, streaming our games, and paying per hour for the privilege of using a controller.

Now, if you’ll excuse me, I’m going to enjoy my four SideWinders while I still can.

Phantom Blade Zero launched digitally for PlayStation 5 and PC via Steam and Epic Games Store on October 29. A physical edition is due out for PlayStation 5 in 2027.

Here is an overview of the game, via S-GAME:

S-GAME presents Phantom Blade Zero, a fusion of classic Wuxia storytelling and exhilarating action powered by Unreal Engine 5. You play as Soul, a warrior with only sixty-six days left to live. Fend off assassins, unravel world-ending conspiracies, and defend your values with your life.

Framed for the death of his master and left with a ruined heart, Soul has sixty-six days to live. Alone and hunted by his former comrades, he moves through a world of shifting loyalties and silent blades—determined to unravel the conspiracy that has condemned him.

Rain mixes with blood, mercy entangles with vengeance. Soul’s journey is one of love, hate, and the fragile search for what it means to have a heart.

A Masterful Blend of Traditional Wuxia, Fantasy, and Folk Horror

Explore a world beyond imagination. Shifting realities, echoes of memories long since passed, augmentation, and beings of higher power await in Phantom Blade Zero.

A rumor, a story, a whisper—every thread a trail to unraveling a larger mystery. Navigate through a web of intrigue and lies to uncover the truth.

Over thirty weapons are yours to wield, with more than twenty unique “Phantom Edges” to mix and match to suit your playstyle.

Defeat powerful foes to obtain their weapons, and with it, their signature techniques. Grow your arsenal and defeat all who stand in your path.

Inspired by the Golden Age of Hong Kong action films, the world of Phantom Blade Zero blends fierce martial arts with machinery, amplifying an exhilarating clash of steel on steel.

Ancient codes meet iron and smoke; tradition thrums to a modern beat. A new style is forged in this melding of mediums. This is Kungfupunk.

Built in Unreal Engine 5 and through the use of state-of-the-art motion capture, Phantom Blade Zero brings together legendary fight choreography from Hong Kong’s Golden Age of martial arts cinema.

Every strike and stance draws from authentic martial arts techniques, captured with the precision of film, is reborn through modern game design.

This is Chinese kungfu reimagined for a new generation.

"My supporters donated $1,000 for me to do a Mario impression"

Super Mario Bros. players have spent years trying to build the perfect speedrun. The race to be the first to achieve the perfect run has escalated dramatically over the past year, and the now-legendary Niftski has just set a new record that's just two frames away from the entire community's ultimate goal. The catch? He didn't actually want to do it – at least not when he did.

"My supporters donated $1,000 for me to do a Mario impression" for an entire Halloween stream, as Niftski explains in the description of his record run on YouTube. He dutifully completed the stream dressed in a Mario hat and fake mustache while doing what he recognizes as "the worst Mario impression of all time."

The entire video is an absolute delight as Niftski slowly recognizes that he's on world record pace while wearing a silly costume and doing a silly voice. "Finally, I just-a had to-a lock in," he says as he warps into level 4-1. The faux facial hair starts to bother him in 4-2, as he complains that "I want to shave-a this thing off because it's-a literally freaking uncomfortable as hell-a."

"I really hope this run dies, by the way," he says as he enters the game's final stages, still on pace for that record. By level 8-3, the penultimate stage, he's getting desperate. "Please have this-a run die," he begs, "I don't-a like it, I don't-a want to get this larping as Mario."

Yet he does indeed secure the world record while-a doing a Mario voice. "It made me not nervous at all," he recognizes, and that might've been the push he needed to set the new record. Still, there are two more frames to shave away before the perfect speedrun finally arrives, and I can only imagine what lengths Niftski might have to go to in order to calm his nerves again.

#3978. Atmosfar is a giddy aerial exploration game after the heart of No Man's Sky, but I'm already trying to escape it

Oh hi there! Why yes, I am free to chat. Please excuse the wind noise, I'm currently tumbling to my doom in Atmosfar, after getting lost in a cloud bank and exhausting my fuel. This kind of thing happens to me regularly in Atmosfar - an open world survival game that plays out across clusters of floating islands, with players scooting about in adorable, propellor-powered airships.

Many of the islands are quite large, with proper landing pads and bases set up by NPC scavengers. Many of them teem with non-human life: rainforests full of nectar droplets and carnivorous plants, meadows of ponderous honking lizards, and mossy grottos where you'll find caches of batteries and possibly get eaten by mantids. It's important to make the most of these larger islands, gathering materials for crafting at your deployable campsite (which straps pleasingly to the back of your whirring fly-mobile). It's particularly important to mine hydrogen crystals you can refine into fuel.

None of that's for me, though! I am a true spirit of the sky. The only fuel I need is my imagination. The only objective marker I acknowledge is the omnidirectional Call to Adventure. Besides, when you do run out of fuel in Atmosfar, you're actually unlocking two exciting minigames. The first consists of leaping from the cockpit and vainly trying to jetpack to the nearest walkable surface. The second consists of racing to overtake your plummeting airship and re-enter the cockpit before you smash into any islands beneath. I'm playing that second minigame right now. Come to papa, my beautiful turboprop son! Ah, balls.

Atmosfar is out in Steam early access today, with plans to stay in early access for at least nine months. I think it has some juice, though I am admittedly already trying to play it against the grain - and at times, trying to do things its technology doesn't quite allow.

It casts you as an interplanetary pioneer who, due to some minor infraction, has been locked up in a factory: a dreary opening area with some corpo-satire elements, from which you are soon liberated by an electrical storm. Busting past the sentry drones, you scramble down a cliffside and discover your very first Wasp hovercar. From there, you have more or less free rein of the game's opening biome, though there's a critical path of tutorials and NPC encounters you'll want to follow for the sake of unlocks, like the jetpack.

The scattered islands do a fair job of luring you from your HUD objectives (the HUD itself is a bit murky, in any case – I struggled to make connections between waypoints and quests in my journal). Even if there's nothing to capital-i Interact with, it's a pleasure to alight on some drifting gobbet of soil and flowers, peer into the crevices, and maybe take a few photos of distant astral mountains.

The searing emptiness all around makes the design of each island feel more precise and careful, gift-wrapped for the player. I find that I'm most interested in the tinier islands, the ones that were presumably a secondary consideration for developers Apog Labs, and maybe handed off to a junior staffer. I gaze at a random grass tuft and try to guess how much ingenuity went into the placement of something many pilots will totally ignore.

I'm already chafing against the survival systems a bit, however. Based on a couple of hours of cloudsteading, Atmosfar's core ingredients aren't particularly novel or involving. There's no tree-chopping, thank god, but you will spend many moments pointing your extractor at a nugget of glowing resourcegook, splitting it into plastic sheets and steel girders and so forth.

Many of the opening missions involve toing and froing between deposits and your airship or camp. It's humdrum stuff. The game's non-player scavengers seem like quest-givers first, characters second. Your inventory size is limited, to begin with. Deeper in, there's the opportunity to construct a huge airbase, the Cloud Cruiser, which I'm really hoping doesn't need refuelling. Although it would be a great joke to accidentally drop one with several co-op buds inside.

I've spent most of my two hours in Atmosfar in headlong retreat from the tutorial quests, trying to reach places I sense I'm not supposed to, without paying my dues to the crafting system. This includes both the ruddier, volcanic areas higher up, which I do believe I can reach, if I bother to refine enough fuel. But I'm more captivated, right now, by what lies beneath.

During a nighttime mission to gather eggs for some outpost chef, I gave into curiosity and aimed my Wasp straight down, spiralling past lonely stalactites with no creature population, into a swirling turquoise abyss full of bare, indistinct rock. As I descended, the game's tech began to creak and fizzle, as though strained by increasing gravity. My ride's exhaust condensed and flattened into glitchy flakes.

I ignored the simulation's protests, holding my course like Ahab aiming a harpoon at Moby Dick's kisser, till a "leaving mission area" reset timer yanked me up short. I ascended to just above the cut-off point, and gawped at the horizon. A juddering white ring enclosed the world, surrounded by wrinkled LIDAR pulses that made me think of thoughts coursing through brain tissue.

Now, this was an adventure. I flapped around a bit, battling turbulence, and managed to land on one of the weirdly unadorned, formless boulders. Who made this? Some procedural generation system, or did somebody actually have to 'hand-craft' these places that are probably not for serious human inquiry or habitation? I shot a few flares over the side and tried to deploy my campsite, but there was too little space on the boulder. Then the sun rose, slowly staining the milky blue fastness pink, and revealing the crisper silhouettes of the properly designed and navigable islands high above.

That last screenshot is my favourite so far - the rosy, rugged beauty of Atmosfar and the bizarre quirks of its technology reaching a strangely persuasive accord. There's only one issue: I've run out of fuel again. I guess I could yeet myself into the void and reset to the nearest landing pad, but that doesn't feel like something a true Spirit of the Sky would do. I guess I'll have to enlist another RPS scribe as a co-op partner and have them come fetch me. Perhaps they can complete the tutorials first and rock up in one of those Cloud Cruiser things. In the meantime, you can get your fill of Atmosfaring via Steam.

"The first thing that got us debating was the necrophiliac scene in the first Outlast. We had a lot of conversations about do we do it? Are we going too far with this? And how does it make sense in this environment? That was a heated conversation."

There are many scenes from Outlast that are burned into my memory, The Groom's sequence in Outlast's Whistleblower DLC, the finger amputation from the first game, or perhaps it was landing on a bunch of baby bones in Outlast 2. There's quite a lot to pick from over two games, a DLC, and the live service The Outlast Trials. But if Philippe Morin, co-founder of Red Barrels, had to pick the scene that made the team really stop and think about whether this was ok he'd go back to the first game.

For those who don't remember, or perhaps have never played the game, or maybe just wiped the encounter from your memory, as the protagonist Miles Upshur is navigating the abandoned Mount Massive Asylum he stumbles across an inmate engaging in necrophilia. It's a pretty startling moment, and was actually the last thing I thought I'd come across, even in an Outlast game. But that was the whole point of that scene.

"We felt like we needed something that's going to make people think that anything can happen in this game," Morin explains. "Then J.T. Petty, [lead writer for Outlast] came up with this whole dialogue of switching things around, having the [necrophiliac] say to you, 'You like to watch? You're fucked up!' So that was a really nice spin because it turned things around. Because obviously, yes, the player is making the choice to watch. So yeah, I mean that's probably the very first sequence that got a bit [heated]."

The only other time Morin can recall where the team spent so long debating whether or not to include a scene actually happened more recently, in The Outlast Trials. Specifically, the decision to include child mannequins instead of animated children in trials like Grind the Bad Apples or Punish the Miscreants.

Morin explains how the team questioned "what to do with the kids? Do we make them mannequins, or do we have actual characters? At the end of the day it's a bunch of polygons moving. But you know, in the player's mind, it's not the same thing. That was probably where we found our limit. Like, no, let's stick with mannequin kids, and not go too far with that."

This was undoubtedly the right decision. There's plenty of extreme moments in The Outlast Trials with objectives like Pervert the Futterman or Despoil the Auction, the gore and horror already present is more than enough to make players feel uneasy as is—trust me.

But as it is with most games, the best decisions tend to be made by the people who know the series best; its devs. "The team is always the first to react to some of these ideas," Morin says. "So sometimes if people feel like it's alright, let's keep pushing in that direction until like maybe the reaction becomes a little too strong.
